topic.angle: A small annual cost gap compounds over decades

card.title: What a one-point fee costs over 30 years

body.question: Two funds earn the same before costs. After costs, one grows 7% a year and the other 6%. Starting from $10,000, about how many dollars bigger is the 7% pile after 30 years?
body.reveal: About $18,700. At 7% a year, $10,000 becomes about $76,100; at 6% it becomes about $57,400. Costs come out of returns every year, so the gap compounds too. These rates are made up to show the maths and are not a forecast or advice.

probes.question: $10,000 grows 7% a year for 30 years, and a second $10,000 grows 6%. About how many dollars bigger is the first pile?
Why does it generally cost less to run an index fund than an actively managed fund?
options: The target index is a known quantity

image_brief.show: File:Electronic stock board in Yaesu, Tokyo 2007.jpg shows an electronic board displaying market data

claims.claim: Index funds generally cost less to run than active funds (probe 2)
claims.quote: Because the composition of a target index is a known quantity, relative to actively managed funds, it costs less to run an index fund.

claims.claim: Costs reduce returns, so the gap compounds
claims.quote: turnover has both explicit and implicit costs, which directly reduce returns on a dollar-for-dollar basis
claims.note: Assumed rates are labelled made up in the card; compounding of the gap is arithmetic.
